t: Day thirty, nine-forty p.m. Above your head a sign: free evenings — zero.
You flip the kitchen light on. Boil the kettle. Take three cups.
No invites.
Brother leaves today. Where, when — you don't know.
But three cups. Kettle boils.
What if every improvement cost you an evening with someone close?
Not money. Not later. An evening: football, film, Grandpa's chess.
Let's rewind thirty days.
You're Mitya, fifteen. Thirty days ago a teacher stops you in the hall.
Me? I mumble.
You mumble, slouch, stare at the floor. You know it. One month to pull yourself together.
At night you rehearse your stage entrance at the bathroom mirror.
In 2006, Princeton psychologists Willis and Todorov showed people face photos for a tenth of a second.
The impression formed fast and barely changed afterwards. That doesn't make it right.
Now, your week. Every evening someone is waiting.
Monday: football, Vovan. Tuesday: fractions, sister. Wednesday: FIFA, brother.
Thursday: chess, Grandpa. Friday: movie, Tyoma. Saturday: board games. Sunday: dinner with Mom.
Checkmate. Nine twenty-five. Bedtime for me.
Grandpa sleeps at nine-thirty. Twenty years straight. Eighty on the twenty-ninth. Remember.
On the thirtieth your brother leaves to study. Farewell at seven, fancy, booked.
In a month you'll choose between Grandpa and the stage. For now, a smaller problem.
Okay. Thirty days. I'll do it.
Morning: the sign still hangs like a price tag. Twenty-nine. Only you see it.
By day you get a haircut. First improvement. A proper cut instead of 'whatever'.
Overhead, a soft click.
Tick.
At seven, your sister drops her fractions notebook. A friend's birthday — she forgot.
Fine. I'll do them.
The sign shows this month's evenings that are still yours. Today included.
Each midnight takes an unspent evening by itself. An improvement takes one more, the nearest free. For the haircut — today.
Haircut: plus. Sister: minus.
You cut your hair. And look crushed.
Tyoma. I've a sign. I pay with evenings.
No sign. Haircut, yes. We'll test.
That's how you get a scientific adviser. With a bun.
Wednesday you start washing your face twice a day. No lotions, just water.
Pick one. Yourself. Tap.
You tap today's cell. Wednesday, FIFA with brother. Tick.
Same day the coach shows a wall exercise for posture. Second improvement.
Saturday, board games, goes. Tick. Two improvements, two evenings.
That night his gamepad snaps in half. Out of nowhere.
Coincidence. Need more data.
Before bed you watch a video on eye contact and practice on the cat. And forget to assign an evening.
Midnight chooses for you. Nearest free: Thursday. Chess with Grandpa.
The bus broke down. Chess next Thursday.
Noting it.
Rule one: every improvement takes one evening. Two improvements, two evenings.
Rule two: you pick the evening. Don't by midnight — the nearest is taken.
Rule three: a meeting on a taken evening fails. The world finds a reason.
Saturday, Mom gets a shift call. The game sits unopened on the shelf.
Three of three. Final.
Tyoma writes big: 'Busy evening — evening without people.' Leaves.
Alone in the kitchen. Light's on.
The neighbour's kid knocks, no bell, as always. With a box of blocks.
Till nine you build. Taller than the fridge.
He's five. Doesn't count.
He leaves. Lights out.
Gaming till three.
Morning. The mirror shows a person who's been shaken a long time.
In 2010 Swedish scientists led by Axelsson photographed 23 adults.
First after normal sleep. Then after a short night and long wakefulness.
Strangers more often called the second photos tired and slightly less healthy. A small but noticeable gap.
And sleep doctors say teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep.
Slept four.
You try a stage entrance at the mirror. 'Good evening' becomes a yawn.
You look like my laptop. At three percent.
Sleep counts too. Pay an evening.
Which?
You scroll. Football, Vovan. Film, Tyoma. Chess. Every evening's taken.
Sleep waits.
This is the first time you refuse to pay.
Evening, dinner with Mom. Nobody cancelled it.
Clothes that fit, not grow-into tees. You give Thursday. Tick.
Voice. Daily you read a page aloud, slow and loud. You give Friday. Tick.
On Thursday Grandpa's house meeting moves. Right onto seven p.m.
Friday Tyoma leaves for the dacha. No movie.
Friday burned again. You know?
For the concert.
You say it so often you almost believe it.
Saturday you give four evenings at once: walks, step and gestures, stage entrance, diction.
Superhero pose? Hands on hips?
Superhero pose: a big test on two hundred people found no hormones. Only confidence.
I'll take the feeling.
Monday Vovan's pitch is flooded. Thursday Grandpa's lift is broken again.
Friday Tyoma has guests from Tula. No film again.
But your back is straight now. Your voice stays up.
You still mumble when nervous. But less.
Anya, from the next desk. You say 'thanks' and don't mumble.
The sign says ten. Eleven days to the concert.
Day twenty, Saturday. The sign says ten. And Tyoma comes without a bun.
Two Fridays. You pay with me.
For the concert.
Said that already.
Tyoma, wait.
He won't wait. First time ever.
One study estimates about ninety hours together to become a friend. To a close one — over two hundred. Roughly, it varies.
You and Tyoma have hours to spare. But you're spending the spare.
Two lost Fridays — six hours of film. You gave them.
Evening: board games fail again. Mom gets called in.
In the kitchen. The light's on.
Sis walks in unasked. Sets two cups of tea, sits opposite.
She asks nothing. Just sits beside you.
You stay quiet till ten. Good quiet.
At night, the fridge: 'Busy evening — evening without people.'
Not instead — together?
Monday you catch your brother by the door.
Run with me Wednesday? Evening.
You give Wednesday. Tick. Eight now. You wait for the break.
Wednesday you run two laps round the park. He overtakes, you don't quit.
Then he gets a new gamepad. You play till night.
The gamepad doesn't crack. Buses run. He never knew there was a risk.
Rule four: do the improvement together, and one evening pays for both.
You rework the plan. Thursday Grandpa teaches you to tie a tie.
The knot is simple. Like chess: think first.
After the tie, chess. Grandpa wins and at nine twenty-five goes to bed.
You can't make up. So you just text Tyoma: 'Be the jury Friday?'
Yes. Strictly.
Didn't it break? No bus, no gamepad?
Nothing.
Friday Tyoma watches your rehearsal. Strict as a jury.
Louder. Slower. Now the movie.
Shared sleep counts?
Not tested.
Day twenty-eight, Sunday. The sign says three. One item left on the fridge: sleep before the concert.
Concert on the thirtieth. Sleep the night before — the twenty-ninth's evening.
Grandpa turns eighty. Rule three. The meeting won't happen.
Grandpa or the stage: your promised choice.
Sleep on the twenty-eighth. Easy.
They shot by day, after a short night and long wakefulness. Here the last night counts.
Then you recall the clock above the chessboard.
Checkmate. Nine twenty-five. Bedtime for me.
Tyoma's shared-sleep question. Test it.
Grandpa, start at six.
Bed at nine-thirty. I'm staying over.
Finally, a proper party.
You tie sleep to the twenty-ninth's evening. With Grandpa. Tick. Two.
Day twenty-nine. All at Grandpa's: cake, candles, chess.
Grandpa tells of queueing for chess sets in 'eighty-three. Heard a hundred times. Everyone listens.
Your brother laughs all evening. The last evening with him in your calendar.
At nine-thirty Grandpa kills the light. You take the couch.
Cell twenty-nine burns two colours. Test passed. The sign says one.
Day thirty, seven a.m. Brother's suit on the chair. And a note.
Jacket's big. Brother's broader. For now.
Brother left at six for documents. You call.
It's off.
The suit is a new improvement. Not together — he's gone. The last evening burns. Farewell at seven.
We'll see.
Tick.
A text arrives: the seven o'clock booking is off.
Five o'clock, assembly hall. Remember the photo study? A tenth of a second.
You step out holding your back as if that tenth decides all. Then the next. Ninety minutes more.
As coached: step. Gesture. Pause.
Good evening. We begin.
You don't mumble. You joke; they laugh where you planned.
You walk home. In your brother's suit.
Zero overhead. Every evening this month is given.
Where he is, and his train, you don't know.
Mom's on shift, sister's at a friend's. Nine thirty-eight. You open the door to an empty flat.
Nine-forty. The kettle boils. The sign says zero. Three cups.
A knock.
On the step: brother, folder, backpack.
Behind him Tyoma. Your concert on his phone.
Filmed it all. No mumbling. Came to say it.
Passing by after the concert, he saw your window lit.
Last, slowly up the stairs, comes Grandpa.
Can't sleep. Once in eighty years.
He sits on a stool and at once sets chess on the table. Pocket, magnetic.
Twenty years Grandpa slept at nine-thirty. Tonight he didn't.
Three guests. Three cups. No invitations.
I just lit the room.
Tyoma goes to the fridge, takes a marker.
No together. Showing up remains.
Plans break, not visits.
Plans work together too. And visits without a call.
Kid with blocks. Sister with cups. Didn't call either.
Kitchen light isn't an invitation. It's in no calendar.
He drains his tea, checks the clock.
Train: eleven-fifty p.m.
The jacket stays on you. Sleeves still a bit long.
You see him off to the taxi. All four. No booking, no schedule.
Grandpa leaves last, after midnight. Promises to sleep at eighty-one.
At home you open next month's calendar.
Empty cells. A month ago you'd be scared. Now you can just walk in.
You write in only Thursdays: chess. The rest — as it goes.
Only you see the sign. Everyone sees the window light.
You turn off the kitchen light. Three cups stay till morning.
Now your turn. Who will you drop in on today, no call?
